newsitem.title: CANADA: Saudi man U.S. wants to question must leave Canada.
newsitem.headline: Saudi man U.S. wants to question must leave Canada.

text.p: The Canadian government issued a conditional order on Wednesday for the deportation of a Saudi man whom the United States wants to question about a bombing that killed 19 U.S. airmen in Saudi Arabia last June.

An immigration official said that once the government decided where to send Hani Abdel-Rahim Hussein al-Sayegh, it would be a formality to send him out of Canada. The leading choices are Saudi Arabia and the United States.

"We are certainly going to pursue this to deport him as quickly and efficiently as we can," David Olson, an official of Canada's Citizenship Ministry, told reporters inside an Ottawa prison after adjudicator G.R. McBrien signed the order.

Canada's Federal Court ruled on May 5 that a security certificate declaring that Sayegh was a terrorist and a danger to Canada was reasonable, but Wednesday's 11-minute hearing was required to issue the deportation order.

Canadian authorities had accused him of being a driver of the truck that exploded on June 25, 1996, at the Khobar Towers, a complex housing U.S. military personnel in eastern Saudi Arabia, and of belonging to the Hizbollah (Party of God).

Sayegh's lawyer, Doug Baum, said he would press Lucienne Robillard, Canada's minister of citizenship and immigration, not to send him to Saudi Arabia on the grounds that he could well be tortured and was certain to be executed, probably without a fair trial.
"I think it's pretty clear to anybody familiar with Saudi Arabia and the Middle East what fate awaits him there," Baum said.

"I think what the consideration for Canada should be is that before you send a man off to what is certainly summary execution, you owe him the decency of at least ensuring he's going to get some due process," he added.
"If he were going to the United States, I would still be very concerned for his safety, but at least we would know that he would get at least some form of judicial process in the United States."

Sayegh, dressed in a blue prison uniform and blue sneakers and with a closely cropped beard, spoke in Arabic and told reporters he was concerned about the legal system in Saudi Arabia and the safety of his family there.
The FBI issued a statement on March 22, four days after Sayegh's arrest in Ottawa, saying it hoped to question him about the bombing.
Baum said it was not yet clear whether the United States had actually sought to have him deported there.
Olson said he was sure high-level negotiations were going on between the United States and Canada.
"The Americans have a very good interest in this client," he said, adding that they were interested in getting him physically into the United States.
Robillard said in March that her concern for the safety of Canadians was greater than the consideration whether a deportee might face the death penalty.

Olson said it would normally take about a week to issue a notice to Sayegh that he is ineligible to be a refugee, after which he would have 15 days to make a written submission to Robillard. Failing a change of mind, she would then deport him.
Baum said Sayegh, a Shi'ite Moslem, denied any involvement in the bombing and had declined to testify in the Federal Court to protect his family.
